def: A bug where untrusted input changes the meaning of a SQL query (input becomes executable SQL).
A query where SQL structure and user-provided values are sent separately, preventing values from becoming syntax.
Giving a user/service only the permissions it needs; limits damage if something goes wrong.
A security event that breaks your security rules or puts systems/data at risk (for example: an account takeover).
The structured process of detecting, containing, fixing, and learning from a security incident.
Planning and setup before something goes wrong (roles, contacts, logging, and tools).
Noticing suspicious activity, confirming it is real, and understanding what is happening.
Stopping or limiting damage during an incident (for example: isolating a host or revoking sessions).
Removing the root cause of an incident (for example: deleting malware, closing an exposed service, or fixing a vulnerability).
Restoring normal operations safely and making sure the issue does not immediately come back.
Documenting what happened and improving systems/processes to prevent repeats.
When an attacker gains control of someone’s account (often via phishing, stolen passwords, or reused credentials).
A login protection that requires an additional factor beyond a password (like an app code or hardware key).
A temporary login state that lets a user stay signed in; attackers can abuse stolen sessions even without the password.
Recording security-relevant events (logins, admin actions, errors) so you can investigate and detect issues.
A notification triggered by suspicious or important events (for example: many failed logins).
The underlying reason something happened (fixing it prevents the same issue from recurring).
A number that helps a computer deliver network traffic to the right program (a service can listen on a port).
A port where a service is listening and reachable over the network.
A program that provides a network capability (web server, SSH, database) and often listens on a port.
A connection-based network protocol focused on reliable delivery.
A message-based network protocol with less delivery guarantee than TCP, often used when speed matters.
A policy that allows or blocks network traffic based on things like IP, port, and protocol.
A security approach where you block traffic/access by default and only allow what you explicitly need.
All the places an attacker can try to interact with or break into (open ports, exposed services, public endpoints).
Information gathering about targets (hosts, ports, services, versions) before attempting an attack.
A technique to check which ports on a host respond, often used to infer what services are reachable.
A device on a network (server, laptop, router, VM) that has an IP address.
Reachable from outside your network; exposure increases risk because more attackers can reach it.
A software update that fixes bugs, including security vulnerabilities.
A tool that detects suspicious activity and raises alerts (it typically does not block traffic).
A tool that detects suspicious activity and can block or stop it automatically.
A one-way function mapping input to a fixed-size output; small input changes produce very different outputs.
Storing a one-way derived value (not the plaintext password) so you can verify logins by hashing again and comparing.
Random per-password data mixed into hashing so identical passwords don’t produce identical hashes.
A tunable setting that makes password hashing intentionally slower to increase the cost of guessing attacks.
A password hashing algorithm designed to be slow and salted, with a configurable cost parameter.
A fast general-purpose hash that is not safe for password storage and is broken for collision resistance.
Two different inputs that produce the same hash output (a property attackers can exploit in some contexts).
A bug where attackers get script to run in a victim’s browser by injecting content into a page.
An XSS variant caused by client-side JavaScript writing untrusted data into the DOM in an unsafe way.
